extracted.intended_audience: Congressional staff, administrative agencies, attorneys, and scholars concerned with federal administrative procedure
extracted.subtask_description: A legislative-history and section-by-section explanation of a proposed Administrative Procedure Act summarizing required public-information duties, differences between rulemaking and adjudication, minimum hearing and decision requirements, examiner roles, limits on sanctions, and judicial-review provisions for federal agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public information requirements (sec. 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must issue as rules certain specified information as to their organization and procedure, and also make available other materials of administrative law; agencies are required to take the initiative in informing the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public-information provisions are of the broadest application; all administrative operations should be disclosed to the public except where secrecy is obviously required or only internal 'housekeeping' arrangements are involved. The bill spells out public information in considerable detail (sec. 3) — a provision the earlier Walter-Logan bill lacked and which is described as an important feature of the present bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between rulemaking and adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill carefully distinguishes between agencies' legislative functions (rulemaking/regulations) and judicial functions (adjudications/orders) and prescribes quite different procedures for each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulemaking (legislative) and adjudication (judicial) are governed by different sections: rules require notice and opportunity to submit views in writing (sec. 4), while adjudications have prescribed modes of hearing and decision when statutes require hearings (sec. 5). The bill aims to avoid conflating quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking notice and opportunity for comment (notice-and-comment)
rubrics_metrics.description: In rulemaking, with certain exceptions, agencies must publish notice and at least permit interested parties to submit their views in writing for agency consideration before the issuance of general regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No hearings are required by the bill for rulemaking unless statutes already provide for them (see sec. 4). The bill requires publication only of 'substantive rules adopted as authorized by law and statements of general policy or interpretations formulated and adopted by the agency for the guidance of the public' (sec. 3(a)). Agencies protested against burdensome pre-rule requirements; the bill limits publication obligations to substantive rules and policy statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjudication — minimum hearing and decision requirements (secs. 7 and 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where existing statutes require hearings for particular adjudications (orders), sections 7 and 8 set forth the minimum requirements for such hearings and how decisions shall be made thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the bill does not require hearings unless statutes already do so, when hearings are statutorily required the bill prescribes the mode of hearing and decision. Section 7 spells out minimum hearing requirements; section 8 governs post-hearing decisions. These provisions create a baseline procedural standard for agency adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners: role, appointment, and tenure (sec. 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill provides for examiners who may preside at hearings and make or participate in decisions; agencies may choose whether examiners make the initial decision or merely recommend one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill relies on independence, salary security, and tenure during good behavior of examiners within the civil-service framework, although earlier committee proposals favored short-term appointments approved by a special office. The bill does not change the operation of the examiner system where statutes provide otherwise (sec. 7(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on administrative powers and sanctions (sec. 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill contains general limitations upon administrative powers and sanctions, particularly in rigorous fields such as licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These limitations are intended to constrain excessive administrative sanctions and power where appropriate. The report notes that the present bill provides some general limitations which previous committee reports did not address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review: simplified remedial standard (sec. 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simplified statement of judicial review designed to afford a remedy for every legal wrong, subject to statutory exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 10 provides for judicial review as a method of enforcing rights, but expressly does not operate where statutes otherwise preclude judicial review or where agency action is by law committed to agency discretion. Judicial-review provisions supplement the administrative provisions rather than replace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional classifications and exemptions (sec. 2(a) and elsewhere)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill is drawn on a functional basis and makes functional classifications and exemptions rather than exempting agencies by name; where one agency or function is shown to need exemption, comparable agencies/functions are exempted in general terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill's scope is 'across the board' except for functional exemptions; no agency is favored by special treatment. Exemptions include agencies composed of representatives of parties and certain war or temporary functions (which remain subject to public-information requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'agency' and scope of coverage (section 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'agency' is defined broadly by excluding legislative, judicial, and territorial authorities and including any other authority regardless of form; certain specific entities are expressly exempted from parts of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition avoids defining agencies by mere form (e.g., department or board) to prevent inadvertent inclusion of mere housekeeping functions or exclusion of those with real power. Agencies composed of representatives of parties are exempted from most provisions except section 3 (public information).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication limited to substantive rules and policy interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill requires publication only of substantive rules adopted as authorized by law and statements of general policy or interpretations formulated and adopted for the public's guidance (sec. 3(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits burdens on agencies by not requiring publication of every internal procedure, while ensuring the public has access to the substantive standards that affect rights and duties. The balance responds to agency concerns about being required to issue rules for every case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bill as outline of minimum essential rights and procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute is intended as an outline of minimum essential rights and procedures; agencies may fill in details so long as they publish them, thereby giving private parties notice of their rights and administrators a simple framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill is brief but not oversimplified and is meant to afford both public notice and administrative uniformity. Its fourfold substantive summary: public information (sec. 3); essentials of proceedings and limits on powers (secs. 4–6 and 9); detailed hearing/decision requirements where statutes require hearings (secs. 7–8 and 11); and simplified judicial review (sec. 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation/segregation of functions (section 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill contains a segregation provision separating certain functions (e.g., separating adjudicative functions from advocacy or investigative functions), though section 5's segregation does not apply to rulemaking and subsection (c) makes additional exemptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies objected to separation of functions, but the present bill carries segregation further than prior proposals. The report notes explicit language preserving agencies' authority to make declaratory rulings in their 'sound discretion' (sec. 5(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-repeal of prior delegations of authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill expressly states that nothing in the Act shall be construed to repeal delegations of authority provided by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assurance was included to address agency concerns about limitations upon delegations of authority; the Act preserves existing delegations while imposing procedural norms, but this does not permit avoidance of examiner or other procedural requirements where applicable.
